citation.title: Ideologically Extreme Candidates in U.S. Presidential Elections, 1948-2012
citation.venue: Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science

standing_assumptions:
The article (The ANNALS of the American Academy of Political and Social Science 667, September 2016, pp. 126–142; printed page = PDF page + 125, so printed p. 126 is PDF p. 1) is an empirical report on the seventeen U.S. presidential elections from 1948 to 2012. It has no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof; its only displayed formula is the voter-centered extremism display on p. 133, and its other formulas are given in running text and in notes. Everything quoted below was read from the page images.
(S1) Outcomes. p. 128 (PDF p. 3): “The dependent variable in musical chairs is incumbent party vote margin, in percentage points, in the U.S. presidential elections from 1952 to 2012. Third-party votes are implicitly included in this measure, which is calculated as (incumbent party percent of the vote) − (challenging party percent of the vote).” p. 129 (PDF p. 4): “The dependent variable in bread and peace is the incumbent party’s share of the two-party vote in the presidential elections from 1952 to 2012. The measure is calculated as: 100*(incumbent votes / (incumbent + challenger votes)).”
(S2) The discounted income variable of bread and peace. p. 128 (PDF p. 3): “While Hibbs, like Achen and Bartels (2016), also employs change in RDI to measure economic performance, bread and peace allows RDI growth from every quarter of a presidential term to factor into the model, albeit discounted over time so that earlier quarters carry less weight. Hibbs applies a decay parameter—$\lambda$, estimated within the model as a number between 0 and 1—to progressively discount economic growth in earlier quarters of the presidential term. This discounting takes the following form: Because the election is held one-third of the way through the 16th quarter of a presidential term, RDI growth in this quarter is down-weighted by $\tfrac13 * \lambda^0$. The 15th quarter of the presidential term is down-weighted by $\lambda^1$, the 14th quarter by $\lambda^2$, and so on for the preceding quarters. The closer the estimate of $\lambda$ is to 1, the smaller the time decay, so that if $\lambda = 1$, economic growth in earlier quarters would matter just as much as economic growth immediately before the election; the closer the estimate of $\lambda$ is to 0, the greater the time decay.$^{5,6}$ Bread and peace consistently estimates $\lambda$ to be about .9, making the voter’s economic memory very long, as opposed to the short-term memory seen in musical chairs.” Note 5, p. 141 (PDF p. 16): “5. This is because $1^{15} = 1^{14} = \ldots = 1^0 = 1$, so all quarters receive an equal weight of 1; and $0^{15} = 0^{14} = \ldots = 0^1 = 0$, but $0^0 = 1$, so all quarters preceding the election quarter receive a weight of 0.” Note 6, p. 141: “6. For comparison, musical chairs could be thought of as having a decay parameter of $\lambda = 1$ for the 14th and 15th quarter, and $\lambda = 0$ for all other quarters.” The paper prints no formula for the variable as a whole and no normalizing denominator.
(S3) Relative candidate extremism. First method, p. 132 (PDF p. 7): “On both the ANES/Rosenstone and the NOMINATE measures of ideological location, liberal positions are scored as negative and conservative positions are scored as positive. […] To do this, we first transform our scale so that positive numbers represent incumbent-party candidates’ ideology (rather than conservative candidates’ ideology), and negative numbers represent challenging-party candidates’ ideology (rather than liberal candidates’ ideology).$^{11}$ Then we take the midpoint between each set of opposing candidates to arrive at a single relative candidate extremism score for each election. With this transformed scale, positive values of our relative candidate extremism variable indicate that the incumbent-party candidate is more extreme than the challenger; negative values indicate that the challenger is more extreme than the incumbent.” (the last sentence runs on to p. 133). Note 11, p. 141 (PDF p. 16): “11. This simply involves taking the absolute value of every candidate’s ideological location score and then multiplying challenging-party candidates’ scores by −1.” Second method, p. 133 (PDF p. 8): “Based on the self-placement and two candidate placement scales—all recentered to a range of −3 to +3—we measure relative incumbent extremism as follows: $$\text{Incumbent extremism} = \left[\begin{array}{l}(\text{Incumbent position} - \text{Voter mean}) + \\ (\text{Challenger position} - \text{Voter mean})\end{array}\right] / 2 = [\text{Incumbent position} + \text{Challenger position}] / 2 - \text{Voter mean}$$ In the special case in which mean voter ideology is 0, this second method of calculating relative candidate extremism reduces to the first.” Five measures, pp. 133–134 (PDF pp. 8–9): “From the ANES data, we can calculate zero-centered and voter-centered relative candidate extremism measures for elections from 1972 to 2012. We can also calculate a zero-centered measure of relative NOMINATE extremism, but lacking a measure of voter location on the NOMINATE scale, we cannot build a voter-centered NOMINATE measure. We thus arrive at five measures of relative incumbent extremism, each of which can be tested in the musical chairs and bread and peace models. […] In testing five measures in each of the two models, we have a total of ten tests of voter sensitivity to extreme candidates in presidential elections.” [The display is the subject of clarity note P039-A001 and is not a target. The score that was computed, and that the targets use, is $(|x_I - m| - |x_C - m|)/2$, where $x_I$ and $x_C$ are the locations of the incumbent-party and challenging-party candidates on the liberal-negative, conservative-positive scale and $m$ is the reference point, 0 or the mean voter self-placement (deposited script 3).]
(S4) The six specifications of Table 2. p. 136 (PDF p. 11): “Panel A of Table 2 uses the musical chairs model as a starting point. The dependent variable is incumbent party vote margin, and RDI is measured using the musical chairs version of the variable: change in RDI per capita immediately prior to the election (quarters 14 and 15). Incumbent party fatigue, measured by the number of years the incumbent party has spent in the White House, is also included in each of the specifications in Panel A. Column A1 replicates the original musical chairs model, with updated data from 1948 to 2012. Column A2 creates a composite model by introducing the war fatalities variable from bread and peace into the original musical chairs model. In column A3, we add our main incumbent party relative candidate extremism variable (the zero-centered, refined ANES/Rosenstone measure) to the composite model built in column A2.” “Panel B of Table 2 starts with the bread and peace model and builds on it in the same manner that Panel A built upon musical chairs. The dependent variable in Panel B is incumbent party share of the two-party vote, and RDI is measured using Hibbs’s definition of the variable, with quarters 1–16 discounted by a decay parameter as described above. The war fatalities variable is included in each of the Panel B specifications. Column B1 replicates the original bread and peace model using updated data from 1952 to 2012. Column B2 incorporates the incumbent fatigue variable from musical chairs to create a composite based on the bread and peace model. Column B3 then adds our main extremism variable to the composite model from column B2.”
Table 2, “Relative Extremism Variable in Baseline Models”, p. 137 (PDF p. 12; printed sideways), as printed, each coefficient followed by its parenthesized entry. Musical Chairs, columns A1 | A2 | A3: “∆ RDI in Q14-15”: 6.40*** (1.4) | 6.38*** (.96) | 6.38*** (1.0). “Incumbent fatigue (yrs. In WH.)”: −1.79*** (.26) | −1.65*** (.32) | −1.65*** (.35). “War fatalities”: blank | −.02 (.03) | −.02 (.03). “Relative extremism”: blank | blank | −.46 (5.19). “Constant”: 9.2 | 8.7 | 8.6. “N of cases”: 17 | 17 | 17. “adjusted r-squared”: .81 | .80 | .79. “RMSQ”: 4.62 | 4.70 | 4.89. Bread & Peace, columns B1 | B2 | B3: “∆ weighted RDI in Q 1-16”: 3.29*** (.52) | 2.82*** (.44) | 2.89*** (.44). “Incumbent fatigue (yrs. In WH.)”: blank | −.46** (.18) | −.41** (.18). “War fatalities”: −.05*** (.01) | −.02 (.01) | −.02 (.01). “Relative extremism”: blank | blank | −2.23 (2.04). “Decay parameter”: .88 (.06) | .83 (.07) | .83 (.07). “Constant”: 46.8 | 50.2 | 49.6. “N of cases”: 16 | 16 | 16. “adjusted r-squared”: .83 | .88 | .88. “RMSQ”: 2.30 | 1.90 | 1.89. “NOTE: Dependent variable for musical chairs is incumbent vote margin. Dependent variable for bread and peace is incumbent vote share. RDI = real disposable income; WH = White House; RMSQ = Root mean squared error. ***$p$ < .01. **$p$ < .05. *$p$ < .10.”
(S5) Residual plots. p. 138 (PDF p. 13): “The residuals from the composite models in columns A2 and B2 represent the variation in vote outcomes that remains unexplained by the three fundamental variables: change in RDI, incumbent fatigue, and war fatalities. Figure 4 plots the residuals from these two composite models against our main relative extremism variable. This provides a picture of how much of the unexplained variance in vote outcomes might be explained by candidate extremism.” Figure 4, “Additional Explanatory Force of Relative Candidate Extremism” (p. 138): two panels, “Musical Chairs composite model” (vertical axis “Vote margin residuals”) and “Bread and Peace composite model” (vertical axis “Vote share residuals”), each plotting election labels against relative incumbent party candidate extremism on the horizontal axis, with a straight line drawn through the points.
(S6) Maximum effects. p. 139 (PDF p. 14): “Table 3 reports the maximum effect of candidate extremism that would be predicted by each of our ten models. All estimates are based on regressions identical in form to those in columns A3 and B3 in Table 2 and fully documented in our replication files. Maximum effect is calculated as the coefficient for the variable × the largest value of that variable.” Table 3, “Maximum Effect Sizes for All Models”, p. 139, as printed, each row giving Maximum effect, Two-tailed $p$-value, $df$ for Musical chairs and then for Bread and peace: “All-voter perception measures”, “(1) Zero-centered”: −0.43, 0.90, 12 | 1.24, 0.39, 10; “(2) Voter-centered”: 1.33, 0.60, 6 | 0.30, 0.85, 5; “Refined voter perception measures”, “(3) Zero-centered”: 0.29, 0.93, 12 | 1.38, 0.30, 10; “(4) Voter-centered”: 2.28, 0.42, 6 | 0.82, 0.64, 5; “(5) NOMINATE locations”: −2.53, 0.69, 3 | 1.14, 0.77, 2.
(S7) Not in the paper. The paper does not say how the models are estimated, does not say what the parenthesized entries of Table 2 are, prints no formula for the weighted income variable and prints no election-level data. These are taken from the deposited replication files (Yale Dataverse 10.60600/YU/PPBAY4, V1.1; staged under staged/code/yale-dataverse-PPBAY4-v1.1/): script 5_Tables1-3_public.R fits Panel A by lm (ordinary least squares, lines 149, 154, 159) and Panel B and the bread and peace half of Table 3 by nls (nonlinear least squares, lines 236, 242, 247, 321, 332, 343, 354, 365); script 6_Figures1-4_public.R draws each line of Figure 4 by lm(resid(file) ~ extremism) (lines 162 and 194); the relative-extremism scores are in ideology_scores_IncPtyCandRelXtrm.csv and ideology_scores_IPCRE-NOMINATE.csv and the regression inputs in data_fig3&4.csv. Where a target uses deposited numbers, each decimal string is taken as the exact rational it denotes, and the numbers are taken as given: no target concerns how the data were constructed. The online appendix cited in note 7 is not staged.
Scope of the targets. None of the headline claims P039-H1 to P039-H8 is a mathematical statement (each is an empirical estimate or an interpretive conclusion), so there is no headline_result target. No finding is rated above Minor (nine confirmed errors, all Minor), so there is no result_touched_by_finding target and every target has priority 3. The seven targets come from the four confirmed errors whose correction changes mathematical content: P039-E001 (the quarter range and exponent range of the discounted income variable: a formula described with sixteen terms and fitted with fifteen, with an exact witness), P039-E002 (a significance statement read off a regression of residuals: an inferential claim that rests on an exact linear counterexample), P039-E004 (the rule “coefficient × the largest value” and the election that note 15 says it selects: the rule as worded and its stated outcome both fail on the deposited scores) and P039-E003 (a standard error in Table 2 that is arithmetically incompatible with the neighbouring printed entries). The other confirmed errors are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement. P039-N006 (one in-text correlation, −.44 for −.45), P039-N008 (three fit statistics in Table 2, Panel B, off by one in the last digit) and P039-N010 (two candidate locations in the worked example of p. 139, 1.58 and −.34 for 1.57 and −.33) are recalculations of reported numbers from the deposited data; the arithmetic of the worked example, $(|-.34| - |1.58|)/2 = -.62$ and $-2.23 \times (-.62) = 1.3826$, holds for the printed pair, and $(|-.33| - |1.57|)/2 = -.62$ for the corrected pair. P039-E008 and P039-N013 are bibliographic. Findings classed as clarity notes (P039-E005, P039-E006, P039-A001, P039-N005), as not confirmed or as undetermined are outside the brief; two of them touch formulas quoted above (P039-E006: note 5’s “equal weight of 1” at $\lambda = 1$; P039-A001: the display on p. 133), and the targets below do not assert the wording those notes question.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The description of the bread and peace income variable of Table 2, Panel B: ‘with quarters 1–16 discounted by a decay parameter as described above’ (p. 136), the row label ‘∆ weighted RDI in Q 1-16’ (Table 2) and the weighting rule of p. 128, as printed; the witnesses are the validators' constructions and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 136 (PDF p. 11), second paragraph of text; Table 2, p. 137 (PDF p. 12); the weighting rule is on p. 128 (PDF p. 3) and note 5 on p. 141 (PDF p. 16)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact refutation of the printed description (the validators' witnesses; not in the paper): the income variable that the text describes gives weight to all sixteen quarters of the term, and the income variable of the fitted models gives weight zero to quarter 1; the two are different functions of the quarterly growth rates.
Notation (not in the paper). For a real $\lambda \ge 0$ and reals $h_1, \dots, h_{16}$ ($h_q$ is RDI growth in quarter $q$ of the presidential term; quarter 16 is the election quarter), with the convention $\lambda^0 = 1$ also at $\lambda = 0$, put $$N_{2:16}(\lambda,h) = \tfrac13 h_{16} + \sum_{k=1}^{14} \lambda^k h_{16-k}, \qquad D_{2:16}(\lambda) = \tfrac13 + \sum_{k=1}^{14} \lambda^k, \qquad G_{2:16} = \frac{N_{2:16}}{D_{2:16}},$$ $$N_{1:16}(\lambda,h) = \tfrac13 h_{16} + \sum_{k=1}^{15} \lambda^k h_{16-k}, \qquad D_{1:16}(\lambda) = \tfrac13 + \sum_{k=1}^{15} \lambda^k, \qquad G_{1:16} = \frac{N_{1:16}}{D_{1:16}}.$$ $N_{1:16}$ is the weighted sum of the printed description: weight $\tfrac13\lambda^0$ on quarter 16 and $\lambda^{16-q}$ on quarter $q$ for $q = 15, 14, \dots, 1$ (“quarters 1–16”; exponents $0, \dots, 15$ as in note 5). $G_{2:16}$ is the expression that multiplies the income coefficient in every bread and peace model of the deposited scripts. [That the fitted models use $G_{2:16}$ is a premise read from the deposited code; it is not part of the formal statement.]
(i) [The fitted variable ignores quarter 1] $N_{2:16}$, $D_{2:16}$ and $G_{2:16}$ do not depend on $h_1$: if $h$ and $h'$ agree in coordinates $2, \dots, 16$, then $G_{2:16}(\lambda,h) = G_{2:16}(\lambda,h')$.
(ii) [The described variable does not ignore it] $N_{1:16}(\lambda,h) - N_{2:16}(\lambda,h) = \lambda^{15} h_1$ and $D_{1:16}(\lambda) - D_{2:16}(\lambda) = \lambda^{15}$.
(iii) [Witness] Take $\lambda = \tfrac12$, $h_1 = 1$ and $h_2 = \dots = h_{16} = 0$. Then $N_{2:16} = 0$ and $G_{2:16} = 0$, while $N_{1:16} = 2^{-15} = \tfrac{1}{32768}$, $D_{1:16} = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{32767}{32768} = \tfrac{131069}{98304}$ and $G_{1:16} = \tfrac{3}{131069} > 0$. So the two variables differ, with or without the normalizing denominator.
(iv) [Second witness, at a decay close to the fitted values] With $\lambda = \tfrac{9}{10}$ and the same $h$: $N_{2:16} = 0$ and $G_{2:16} = 0$, while $N_{1:16} = \big(\tfrac{9}{10}\big)^{15} = \tfrac{205891132094649}{10^{15}}$, $D_{1:16} = \tfrac{22440939433444477}{3 \cdot 10^{15}}$ and $G_{1:16} = \tfrac{617673396283947}{22440939433444477} > 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The weighting rule, p. 128 (PDF p. 3), and notes 5 and 6: standing assumption (S2). The description of the fitted variable, p. 136 (PDF p. 11): “The dependent variable in Panel B is incumbent party share of the two-party vote, and RDI is measured using Hibbs’s definition of the variable, with quarters 1–16 discounted by a decay parameter as described above.” The row label in Table 2, p. 137 (PDF p. 12), Bread & Peace panel: “∆ weighted RDI in Q 1-16”. The fitted decay parameters, Table 2, row “Decay parameter”: .88 (.06), .83 (.07), .83 (.07).
Not in the paper. (a) The normalizing denominator and the expression $G_{2:16}$: in the deposited scripts the income term of every bread and peace model is `bRDI*( ( ((d0^0)/3)*h16 + (d0^1)*h15 + (d0^2)*h14 + (d0^3)*h13 + (d0^4)*h12 + (d0^5)*h11 + (d0^6)*h10 + (d0^7)*h9 + (d0^8)*h8 + (d0^9)*h7 + (d0^10)*h6 + (d0^11)*h5 + (d0^12)*h4 + (d0^13)*h3 + (d0^14)*h2 )/(1/3+d0+d0^2+d0^3+d0^4+d0^5+d0^6+d0^7+d0^8+d0^9+d0^10+d0^11+d0^12+d0^13+d0^14))`, with `d0` the decay parameter $\lambda$ (spacing normalized here): 5_Tables1-3_public.R lines 236, 242, 247 (Table 2, B1 to B3) and 321, 332, 343, 354, 365 (Table 3, bread and peace), and 6_Figures1-4_public.R line 180 (Figure 4, panel B). Neither `h1` nor `d0^15` occurs in any of the nine. (b) The quarter index: script 5, lines 74–75 and 193–210, defines `h1`, …, `h16` as $400\log(\mathrm{RDI}_t/\mathrm{RDI}_{t-1})$ over the sixteen quarters leading up to the election, in chronological order (for the 2012 election, 2009Q1 to 2012Q4), so `h1` is growth in the first quarter of the term; it is present for all sixteen elections of 1952–2012 in data_fig3&4.csv. (c) $G_{1:16}$ is the validators' reading of the printed description with the scripts' normalization extended by the quarter-1 weight; the printed description fixes the weights and not the denominator, which is why (ii) and (iii) are also stated for the unnormalized sums.
canonical_claim.note: P039-E001 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): the reader is told that the income variable covers quarters 1–16 when every fitted model uses quarters 2–16; correcting the description changes no number. Sol's verdict: confirmed (two validators, both upheld on rerun), false as printed and under the natural reading, evidence an exact counterexample. The witness in (iii) is the second validator's ($\lambda = 1/2$; v2/artifact/derivation.md, section 5) and the one in (iv) is the first validator's ($\lambda = 9/10$; v1/artifact/derivation.md, step 7); both were recomputed in rational arithmetic when this list was fixed. The formal content is (i)–(iv), a statement about two explicit rational functions; the link to the paper's fits is the premise that the nine deposited formulas are $G_{2:16}$, which the validators checked by parsing the scripts and which was read again in the staged scripts for this list. Not established: which quarter range Hibbs (2012) used (the source is not staged), or whether the omission of quarter 1 was intended. On the deposited growth rates, taken as exact decimals, $G_{1:16} \ne G_{2:16}$ at $\lambda = 9/10$ in each of the sixteen elections (validators; recomputed), which is corroboration and not part of the target. The finding bears on headline claims P039-H3 and P039-H6 through Table 2, Panel B.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The description of the bread and peace income variable (p. 128, p. 136, the Table 2 row label and note 5), corrected: quarters 2–16, with exponents 0 to 14
canonical_claim.location: p. 136 (PDF p. 11); Table 2, p. 137 (PDF p. 12); p. 128 (PDF p. 3); note 5, p. 141 (PDF p. 16)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P039-E001, smallest_repair), verbatim: “Explicitly disclose that these analyses exclude Q1 and use Q2–16; change the quarter range on p. 136 and the Table 2 Bread & Peace row label to 2–16; clarify the implemented range in the p. 128 discussion. If note 5 describes this implementation, end its power sequence at 14 instead of 15. This preserves the fitted results. Alternatively, implement the originally stated Q1–16 predictor by adding lambda^15*h1 to the numerator and lambda^15 to the denominator in all nine formulas, then refit and update Table 2B, the Bread & Peace half of Table 3, Figure 4B, and the numerical discussion; remove B3 fatigue's p<.05 marker.”
Corrected text (validated.json, prior_correction.corrected_text, first alternative): “In the analyses reported here, the weighted income-growth predictor uses quarters 2–16 of each presidential term; quarter 1 is excluded. Quarter 16 receives weight 1/3, quarters 15 through 2 receive weights lambda through lambda^14, and the weighted sum is divided by 1/3+sum_{k=1}^{14}lambda^k. Label the Table 2 Bread & Peace income row 'Delta weighted RDI in Q 2-16.'”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis. Notation as in P039-T1: $\lambda \ge 0$ real, $h = (h_1, \dots, h_{16}) \in \mathbb{R}^{16}$, $\lambda^0 = 1$ also at $\lambda = 0$.
(i) [Corrected definition] The income variable of the fitted models is $$G_{2:16}(\lambda,h) = \frac{\tfrac13 h_{16} + \sum_{k=1}^{14} \lambda^k h_{16-k}}{\tfrac13 + \sum_{k=1}^{14} \lambda^k},$$ with weight $\tfrac13$ on quarter 16, weight $\lambda^{16-q}$ on quarter $q$ for $q = 15, \dots, 2$ (exponents 1 to 14) and no weight on quarter 1. For every $\lambda \ge 0$ the denominator satisfies $D_{2:16}(\lambda) \ge \tfrac13 > 0$, so $G_{2:16}(\lambda,h)$ is defined, and it does not depend on $h_1$.
(ii) [Exact relation to the sixteen-quarter variable of the printed description] For every $\lambda \ge 0$ and every $h$: $N_{1:16} = N_{2:16} + \lambda^{15} h_1$, $D_{1:16} = D_{2:16} + \lambda^{15}$, and $$G_{1:16}(\lambda,h) - G_{2:16}(\lambda,h) = \frac{\lambda^{15}\,\big(h_1 - G_{2:16}(\lambda,h)\big)}{D_{1:16}(\lambda)}.$$ Hence $G_{1:16}(\lambda,h) = G_{2:16}(\lambda,h)$ if and only if $\lambda = 0$ or $h_1 = G_{2:16}(\lambda,h)$.
(iii) [The two limiting cases of note 5, with the exponents running from 0 to 14] At $\lambda = 1$: $1^{14} = 1^{13} = \dots = 1^0 = 1$, the weights are $\tfrac13$ on quarter 16 and $1$ on each of quarters $15, \dots, 2$, $D_{2:16}(1) = \tfrac{43}{3}$ and $G_{2:16}(1,h) = \tfrac{3}{43}\big(\tfrac13 h_{16} + \sum_{q=2}^{15} h_q\big)$. At $\lambda = 0$: $0^{14} = \dots = 0^1 = 0$ and $0^0 = 1$, every quarter before the election quarter has weight 0, $D_{2:16}(0) = \tfrac13$ and $G_{2:16}(0,h) = h_{16}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The printed passages being repaired (p. 128, p. 136, the Table 2 row label, note 5) and the notation $N$, $D$, $G$ are in P039-T1 and standing assumption (S2). Not in the paper: the normalizing denominator $\tfrac13 + \sum_{k=1}^{14}\lambda^k$ and the quarter index of $h_1, \dots, h_{16}$, both from the deposited scripts (P039-T1, definitions_needed (a) and (b)).
canonical_claim.note: Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair; prior_correction.status ‘correct’; second validator's repair to the same effect). Repair cost recorded by Sol: none; the documentary repair describes the specification that was fitted and changes no estimate, assumption or conclusion. The correction is to a definition, so there is no theorem of the paper to prove: the expected formalization is the definition in (i) with its two properties, the identity in (ii) (validators' derivations, v1 step 6 and v2 section 4, where it is also checked symbolically) and the two evaluations in (iii). Item (iii) states the weights as they are: at $\lambda = 1$ the election quarter keeps its factor $\tfrac13$, so the quarters do not all receive the same weight; note 5's phrase “all quarters receive an equal weight of 1” is the subject of clarity note P039-E006 and is not asserted here. The alternative repair (keep ‘quarters 1–16’ and refit with $G_{1:16}$) changes fitted numbers (validators: B3 extremism −2.2285 to −2.2999, approximate $p$ .301 to .294; B3 fatigue $p$ .0466 to .0501; Figure 4B line $p$ .2587 to .2520; all five bread and peace extremism coefficients stay negative and far from significance); those are nonlinear least-squares fits to the deposited data and are not a formal target. (i)–(iii) were recomputed when this list was fixed: the identity in (ii) on 200 random rational inputs, and $D_{2:16}(1) = 43/3$, $D_{2:16}(0) = 1/3$ exactly.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: p. 138, last sentence, with Figure 4, panel B: the two-tailed p-value of the line fitted to the B2 residuals (.26), read as a test of the statistical significance of candidate extremism once the fundamentals are accounted for; the witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 138 (PDF p. 13), last sentence, and Figure 4, panel B; compare Table 2, column B3 (p. 137, PDF p. 12) and Table 3, row (3) (p. 139, PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact refutation of the procedure (the validator's witness; not in the paper): the ordinary $t$ test of the slope in a regression of first-stage residuals on a raw regressor, referred to $n - 2$ degrees of freedom, is not the test of that regressor's coefficient in the model that also contains the first-stage regressors. On the same data the two tests can disagree at the 5% level, the two slopes can differ, and under the Gaussian null the residual-regression statistic does not have the $t_{n-2}$ distribution.
Setting (ordinary least squares, conventional standard errors). For a design matrix $A$ with $n$ rows and full column rank $p$ and a response $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$: $\hat\beta = (A^\top A)^{-1} A^\top c$, $\mathrm{SSE} = \|c - A\hat\beta\|^2$, degrees of freedom $n - p$, squared standard error of the last coefficient $\mathrm{SE}^2 = \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-p}\,\big[(A^\top A)^{-1}\big]_{pp}$, and $t = \hat\beta_p / \mathrm{SE}$. Let $n = 6$, $\mathbf{1} = (1,1,1,1,1,1)^\top$, $u = (1,-1,0,0,0,0)^\top$, $v = (0,0,1,-1,0,0)^\top$, $w = (0,0,0,0,1,-1)^\top$; first-stage design $Z = [\mathbf{1}, u]$; $M = I - Z(Z^\top Z)^{-1} Z^\top$; outcome $y = u + \tfrac32 v + w = (1, -1, \tfrac32, -\tfrac32, 1, -1)^\top$; first-stage residual $r = My$.
(i) $Z^\top Z = \mathrm{diag}(6, 2)$, $M$ is symmetric and idempotent of rank 4, $r = \tfrac32 v + w = (0, 0, \tfrac32, -\tfrac32, 1, -1)^\top$ and $\|r\|^2 = \tfrac{13}{2}$.
(ii) [Same slope and same residuals, different tests] Take $x = v$. Residual regression (response $r$, design $[\mathbf{1}, x]$): coefficients $(0, \tfrac32)$, residual vector $w$, $\mathrm{SSE} = 2$, 4 degrees of freedom, $\mathrm{SE}^2 = \tfrac14$, $t^2 = 9$. Full regression (response $y$, design $[\mathbf{1}, u, x]$): coefficients $(0, 1, \tfrac32)$, residual vector $w$, $\mathrm{SSE} = 2$, 3 degrees of freedom, $\mathrm{SE}^2 = \tfrac13$, $t^2 = \tfrac{27}{4}$.
(iii) [The two tests disagree at the 5% level] For $t \ge 0$ the two-sided tail probability of Student's $t_4$ is $1 - \tfrac32 z + \tfrac12 z^3$ with $z = t/\sqrt{4 + t^2}$; at $t = 3$ it is $p_{\mathrm{res}} = 1 - \frac{45}{13\sqrt{13}}$, and $p_{\mathrm{res}} < \tfrac{1}{20}$ because $900 > 247\sqrt{13}$, that is $900^2 = 810000 > 793117 = 247^2 \cdot 13$. For $t \ge 0$ the two-sided tail probability of Student's $t_3$ is $1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\big(\arctan q + \frac{q}{1+q^2}\big)$ with $q = t/\sqrt{3}$; at $t = \tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}$ (so $q = \tfrac32$, and $\arctan\tfrac32 = \tfrac{\pi}{4} + \arctan\tfrac15$) it is $p_{\mathrm{full}} = \tfrac12 - \frac{2}{\pi}\big(\arctan\tfrac15 + \tfrac{6}{13}\big)$, and $p_{\mathrm{full}} > \tfrac12 - \tfrac23\big(\tfrac15 + \tfrac{6}{13}\big) = \tfrac{23}{390} > \tfrac{1}{20}$ because $\arctan\tfrac15 < \tfrac15$ and $\pi > 3$. So the test of the line through the residuals rejects at the 5% level and the test of the coefficient in the full model does not ($p_{\mathrm{res}} \approx .0399$, $p_{\mathrm{full}} \approx .0805$).
(iv) [The slopes differ when the raw regressor is correlated with a first-stage regressor] Take instead $x = u + v$, with the same $Z$, $y$ and $r$. Residual regression of $r$ on $[\mathbf{1}, x]$: slope $\tfrac34$, $\mathrm{SSE} = \tfrac{17}{4}$, $t^2 = \tfrac{36}{17}$ on 4 degrees of freedom. Full regression of $y$ on $[\mathbf{1}, u, x]$: coefficients $(0, -\tfrac12, \tfrac32)$, so the coefficient of $x$ is $\tfrac32$, with $\mathrm{SSE} = 2$ and $t^2 = \tfrac{27}{4}$ on 3 degrees of freedom. Here $x^\top M x = 2$, $x^\top x = 4$ and $\tfrac34 = \tfrac32 \cdot \tfrac24$.
(v) [Wrong reference distribution under the null] Let $x = v$ and $y = Z\gamma + \varepsilon$ with $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I_6)$, $\sigma > 0$. Then the residual-regression statistic is $T_{\mathrm{res}} = U/\sqrt{V/4}$, where $U = v^\top\varepsilon/(\sigma\sqrt2) \sim N(0,1)$ and $V \sim \chi^2_3$ is independent of $U$; that is, $T_{\mathrm{res}} = \sqrt{4/3}\;T$ with $T \sim t_3$. Hence $E[T_{\mathrm{res}}^2] = \tfrac43 \cdot 3 = 4$, whereas a $t_4$ variable has second moment $\tfrac{4}{4-2} = 2$: $T_{\mathrm{res}}$ is not $t_4$ distributed.

canonical_claim.note: P039-E002 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): the .26 is the nominal $p$-value of a line through first-stage residuals, which is not a valid test of extremism given the fundamentals; the paper itself reports the full-model value (.30) and both are far from significance. Sol's verdict: confirmed in part, upheld on rerun; false_as_printed is false (the literal number .26 is the correct nominal output for the plotted line) and false_under_natural_reading is true (the paragraph uses it to judge statistical significance after accounting for the fundamentals). The target therefore refutes the inferential procedure, not an arithmetic statement of the paper, and it is not a claim that the paper's conclusion changes at any level. The algebraic core is (i), (ii) and (iv): exact rational least-squares computations. (iii) needs the two closed-form tails, which may be taken as the definitions of the two $p$-values, and then two elementary inequalities. (v) is distributional; its algebraic content is that in case (ii) the two statistics satisfy $t_{\mathrm{res}}^2 = \tfrac43\,t_{\mathrm{full}}^2$ identically in $y$ (P039-T4 (e)), so that $t_{\mathrm{res}}$ is $\sqrt{4/3}$ times a statistic with the $t_3$ distribution. When this list was fixed, (i), (ii) and (iv) were recomputed in exact arithmetic, the two closed-form tails were checked against numerical integration of the $t_4$ and $t_3$ densities at several points, and the inequalities and moments were recomputed. The validator's script is artifact/exact_check.py (output in exact-output.txt). The finding bears on headline claim P039-H3.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: p. 138, last sentence, as repaired by Sol: the line of Figure 4, panel B is descriptive, and the test of extremism given the fundamentals is the test of its coefficient in the full model B3 (formal content: the algebra that relates the two regressions)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P039-E002, smallest_repair), verbatim: “Keep Figure 4B as a descriptive residual plot. Replace the significance sentence with: 'The negative slope in panel B is descriptive. In the full bread and peace composite model B3, the extremism coefficient is -2.23, with an approximate two-tailed p-value of .30 on ten degrees of freedom; it remains well short of statistical significance.'”
Formal content of the corrected claim (exact for linear least squares; the validator's derivation, steps 1–8). Let $Z$ be a real $n \times k$ matrix of full column rank whose column space contains $\mathbf{1}$, let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ lie outside the column space of $Z$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $n > k + 1$. Put $P = Z(Z^\top Z)^{-1} Z^\top$, $M = I - P$, $r = My$ (the first-stage residual), $\bar x = \mathbf{1}^\top x / n$, $x_c = x - \bar x\,\mathbf{1}$, $S_M = x^\top M x$ and $S_c = x_c^\top x_c$.
(a) $P^\top = P = P^2$, $M^\top = M = M^2$, $MZ = 0$, $\mathbf{1}^\top r = 0$, $M x_c = M x$, $x_c^\top r = x^\top r = x^\top M y$, and $S_c = S_M + \|P x_c\|^2$. Hence $0 < S_M \le S_c$, with $S_M = S_c$ if and only if $P x_c = 0$, that is, if and only if the centered regressor is orthogonal to every column of $Z$.
(b) [The line through the residuals] The least-squares fit of $r$ on $[\mathbf{1}, x]$ has slope $a = x^\top r / S_c$ and intercept $-a\bar x$, and its error sum of squares is $\mathrm{SSE}_{\mathrm{res}} = \|r\|^2 - (x^\top r)^2 / S_c$.
(c) [The full model] The least-squares fit of $y$ on $[Z, x]$ is unique; its coefficient on $x$ is $b = x^\top r / S_M$ and its error sum of squares is $\mathrm{SSE}_{\mathrm{full}} = \|r\|^2 - (x^\top r)^2 / S_M$.
(d) [Attenuation] $a = b\,S_M / S_c$. So $a$ and $b$ have the same sign, $|a| \le |b|$, and $a = b$ if and only if $b = 0$ or $P x_c = 0$; and $\mathrm{SSE}_{\mathrm{full}} \le \mathrm{SSE}_{\mathrm{res}}$.
(e) [The two $t$ statistics] With conventional standard errors, $\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{res}}^2 = \frac{\mathrm{SSE}_{\mathrm{res}}}{(n-2)\,S_c}$ on $n - 2$ degrees of freedom and $\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{full}}^2 = \frac{\mathrm{SSE}_{\mathrm{full}}}{(n-k-1)\,S_M}$ on $n - k - 1$ degrees of freedom. If $\mathrm{SSE}_{\mathrm{full}} > 0$, then $$t_{\mathrm{res}}^2 = \frac{a^2}{\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{res}}^2} = \frac{(n-2)\,(x^\top r)^2}{S_c\|r\|^2 - (x^\top r)^2}, \qquad t_{\mathrm{full}}^2 = \frac{b^2}{\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{full}}^2} = \frac{(n-k-1)\,(x^\top r)^2}{S_M\|r\|^2 - (x^\top r)^2},$$ and therefore $\frac{t_{\mathrm{res}}^2}{n-2} \le \frac{t_{\mathrm{full}}^2}{n-k-1}$. If moreover $P x_c = 0$, then $a = b$, the two fits have the same residual vector, and $t_{\mathrm{res}} = \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-k-1}}\;t_{\mathrm{full}}$: the same slope and the same residuals, with the error sum of squares divided by $n - 2$ in place of $n - k - 1$, so that $|t_{\mathrm{res}}| > |t_{\mathrm{full}}|$ whenever $k \ge 2$ and $t_{\mathrm{full}} \ne 0$.
(f) [Why the residual line has no $t_{n-2}$ reference] If $y = Z\gamma + \varepsilon$ with $\sigma > 0$, $E\varepsilon = 0$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I_n$, then $r = M\varepsilon$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(r) = \sigma^2 M$, a matrix of rank $n - k$ and not $\sigma^2 I_n$. If in addition $\varepsilon$ is Gaussian with $\sigma > 0$, then $t_{\mathrm{full}}$ has the $t_{n-k-1}$ distribution; when $P x_c = 0$, by (e), $t_{\mathrm{res}}$ is $\sqrt{(n-2)/(n-k-1)}$ times a $t_{n-k-1}$ variable, which for $k \ge 2$ is not $t_{n-2}$ distributed (P039-T3 (v) is the case $n = 6$, $k = 2$).
(g) [Application to the paper; not a formal part] In the paper $n = 16$ and the first stage B2 has five fitted parameters (constant, income coefficient, incumbent fatigue, war fatalities, decay parameter), so the line of Figure 4, panel B is referred to $n - 2 = 14$ degrees of freedom and the coefficient in B3 to $16 - 6 = 10$, the count printed in Table 3. B2 and B3 are nonlinear in the decay parameter, so (a)–(f) apply to them through the linearization at the fitted parameters, with $Z$ replaced by the $16 \times 5$ Jacobian of the B2 mean function. The corrected sentence reports the test that (c) and (e) describe: the coefficient −2.23 with standard error 2.04 in B3 and its approximate two-tailed $p$-value .30 on ten degrees of freedom.

canonical_claim.statement:
Exact refutation (the validators' calculations on the deposited relative-extremism scores, taken as exact decimals; the scores are not printed in the paper).
Notation. For measure $j \in \{1, \dots, 5\}$ (the rows of Table 3) and election year $t$, $x_{j,t}$ is the incumbent-party relative candidate extremism score, defined for $t \in T_j$: $T_1 = T_3 = \{1948, 1952, \dots, 2012\}$ (17 elections), $T_2 = T_4 = \{1972, 1976, \dots, 2012\}$ (11 elections) and $T_5 = \{1960, 1964, 1968, 1972, 1984, 1996, 2004, 2008\}$ (8 elections). The 64 values are listed in definitions_needed.
(i) [Note 15 fails for both voter-centered measures] $x_{2,1972} = -0.51177218671487$ and $x_{2,1980} = -0.171462108121506$, so $|x_{2,1972}| - |x_{2,1980}| = \frac{85077519648341}{250000000000000} > 0$. $x_{4,1972} = -0.60215659702977$ and $x_{4,1980} = -0.294347822983647$, so $|x_{4,1972}| - |x_{4,1980}| = \frac{307808774046123}{1000000000000000} > 0$. Hence for measures (2) and (4) the score of greatest magnitude is not the 1980 score, and the four maximum effects in rows (2) and (4) of Table 3 (one for each model in each row) are not computed from the 1980 election; the statement “For the eight measures based on ANES/Rosenstone, this was the 1980 election” is false for four of the eight.
(ii) [The largest value in signed order is not the value used] $x_{3,1980} = -0.621023999873778 < 0 < 0.27380029103004 = x_{3,1984}$, so the largest value of the zero-centered refined variable does not occur in 1980 and is not $-.62$. For every measure the largest value in signed order is positive: $\max_t x_{1,t} = x_{1,1984} = 0.235890938802093$, $\max_t x_{2,t} = x_{2,1996} = 0.336875932107128$, $\max_t x_{3,t} = x_{3,1984} = 0.27380029103004$, $\max_t x_{4,t} = x_{4,2012} = 0.34241131733838$ and $\max_t x_{5,t} = x_{5,1968} = 0.116$. Under the rule as worded the score “employed in these calculations” would therefore be positive for all five variables, against “always negative” in the next paragraph of p. 139; for the worked example it would give $-2.23 \times 0.27380029103004 = -\frac{1526436622492473}{2500000000000000} < 0$, not the printed $+1.38$.
